note: Built by registry/build.py — edit the parts there, not this file. `source` blocks are read by scripts/bake-layers.mjs in CI; the browser ignores them.

groups.label: The regulatory floodplains
groups.blurb: New York City has had two simultaneously-operative, mutually inconsistent regulatory floodplains for over a decade. Turn both on, then put Sandy on top.

groups.label: Future floodplains & sea level rise
groups.blurb: Projections, not forecasts. Every one carries a scenario and a horizon — read the labels before you read the map.

groups.label: What the water actually did
groups.blurb: Sandy, Ida, and the sensors watching for the next one.

groups.label: Rainfall, stormwater & the sewer
groups.blurb: The flooding FEMA's product does not describe — and the infrastructure the City maps but does not publish.

groups.label: The waterfront edge
groups.blurb: Where the city meets the water, who may stand there, and what holds it in place.

groups.label: The harbour as worked space
groups.blurb: Charted by the navy, dredged by the Army, and largely absent from the municipal commons.

groups.label: Buildings & exposure
groups.blurb: Freeboard is first-floor elevation minus base flood elevation. No other combination of layers gives it.

groups.label: Vulnerability & environmental justice
groups.blurb: Redlining under the floodplain, over the EJ areas. Three layers, one publisher.

groups.label: Terrain, bathymetry & imagery
groups.blurb: Vertical datum is NAVD88 throughout. Do not mix it with MLLW or MHHW without saying so.

groups.label: Zoning, jurisdiction & the coastal zone
groups.blurb: The gap between a shapefile and a regulation is itself the lesson.

groups.label: Confirmed absent
groups.blurb: Each of these was searched for and is not published. They are not gaps in this site; they are gaps in the public record, and they are the best teaching material in the survey.

layers.label: 2015 Preliminary FIRM
layers.fields: Flood zone, base flood elevation (STATIC_BFE), zone subtype
layers.notes: The floodplain the NYC Building Code requires for new and substantially improved buildings. FEMA agreed in October 2016 that its models overstated flood elevations by one to two and a half feet citywide, and committed to reissue. No revised maps have been adopted.

layers.label: 2007 Effective FIRM
layers.fields: Flood zone, base flood elevation, zone subtype
layers.notes: The floodplain flood insurance rates actually run off. Simultaneously operative with the 2015 Preliminary FIRM, and inconsistent with it.

layers.label: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer
layers.fields: Flood hazard zones, base flood elevations, cross sections, LOMRs
layers.notes: 32 sublayers, EPSG:4269, maxRecordCount 2000. The bi-state product — this is how New Jersey gets a regulatory floodplain here. WFS caps at 1,000 features: page or tile by bbox.

layers.label: FEMA preliminary / pending NFHL
layers.notes: What FEMA proposes but has not adopted. Put it beside the effective layer and the appeal history becomes visible.

layers.label: FEMA National Risk Index (census tract)
layers.fields: Composite risk, expected annual loss, social vulnerability, community resilience, by hazard
layers.notes: Clip by FIPS 36005 / 36047 / 36061 / 36081 / 36085 for the five boroughs, and the NJ counties for the other side of the harbour. Shapefiles use -9999 for nulls — cast before you average.

source.note: county and tract, CSV / Shapefile / FileGDB

layers.label: NYS Sea Level Rise & Future Floodplain Extent
layers.scenarioNote: 32 floodplains: 8 sea-level-rise increments against 4 annual-chance events. No licence is stated anywhere for this dataset — confirm with NYSERDA before re-serving publicly.
layers.license: NONE STATED — verify before public re-serving

layers.label: DCP future floodplains
layers.scenarioNote: All four are built on the 2015 Preliminary FIRMs, which the City successfully appealed — so they overstate depth by 1 to 2.5 ft. They remain the City's published future floodplains regardless. The 2080s and 2100 versions were stripped to geometry and an Id.

layers.label: Mean monthly high water
layers.scenarioNote: The best proxy in the survey for chronic tidal — sunny-day — flooding. Pair it with the Flood Vulnerability Index's tid_* fields and ask which blocks are wet on an ordinary Tuesday, no storm involved.

layers.label: Future floodplain 2080s, 100-yr (NPCC)
layers.notes: The one DCP future-floodplain service that permits Extract as well as Query.

layers.label: Coastal surge floodplain (MOCEJ)
layers.scenarioNote: MOCEJ publishes coastal surge out to the 2150s — further than any other City product here. Almost none of the account's 255 items carry licenceInfo.

layers.label: NOAA sea level rise depth
layers.scenarioNote: 66 depth rasters for New York at half-foot steps, plus 63 connectivity rasters that distinguish water actually connected to the sea from bathtub artefacts. Every folder ships a URLlist file, so the whole set is trivially scriptable. For a vector pipeline use the merged polygons instead.

layers.label: NOAA SLR merged inundation polygons
layers.notes: The vector route into NOAA's sea-level-rise product, and the cleanest bi-state coverage in the survey.

layers.label: NOAA high-tide flooding extent
layers.notes: Cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs. The Battery is forecast 16–22 flood days in 2026–27; 9 were observed in 2025–26, the lowest since 2016.

layers.label: Sandy inundation zone (2012)
layers.notes: Field-verified through February 2013. Historical — it will never update. Where the water actually went, against three maps that each claim to say where it would go. Use the split-polygon attachment: the single multipolygon kills tiling performance.

layers.label: Sandy high-water marks & storm-tide sensors
layers.fields: Peak elevation, sensor type, deployment and recovery times
layers.notes: 38 storm-surge sensors and 300+ high-water marks. All ten coastal tide gages in southeastern New York exceeded major flood thresholds; peaks ran 7.38 to 11.75 ft. Provisional data — fine for teaching, not for a published risk claim. The same viewer holds Ida's high-water marks.

layers.label: FloodNet street sensors
layers.fields: sensor_id, date installed, tidally influenced, street, borough, NTA, lowest point height delta
layers.notes: 479 live street sensors. CUNY co-leads this, which makes it the obvious partner for the course.

layers.label: FloodNet flood events
layers.fields: Max depth, time to max, drain time, duration above 4 / 12 / 24 inches
layers.notes: The events table has no geometry of its own — join on sensor_id. Time-to-max and drain time are the two fields that turn a flood map into a flood story.

layers.label: 311 flooding complaints
layers.scenarioNote: 311 measures reporting, not flooding. Differential propensity to call — by tenure, immigration status, language, and prior experience of non-response — is the classic confound, and it is exactly what ethnography can address and the API cannot. Note also that Sandy (Oct 2012) lives in dataset 76ig-c548 and Ida (Sep 2021) in erm2-nwe9: any before-and-after comparison crosses two datasets.

layers.label: NYC stormwater flood maps
layers.scenarioNote: This is the Ida layer — the pluvial one. Map Ida's deaths and basement flooding against the FEMA floodplain and there is almost no overlap. That is the finding, not an error: FEMA's product is coastal.

layers.label: Catch basins
layers.notes: 154,212 points and no condition field. A density layer, not a maintenance layer — which is itself the point when you set it beside 44,593 catch-basin-clogged complaints.

layers.label: Green infrastructure assets
layers.fields: Asset type, status, sewer type, outfall, receiving waterbody, constructed date
layers.notes: Rich enough to ask when as well as where — one of the few City layers that is.

layers.label: MS4 outfalls
layers.notes: With catch basins, the only sewer geometry the City releases. There is no CSO outfall layer, no sewer mains, no regulators, no interceptors.

layers.label: MS4 drainage areas
layers.notes: Which outfall a given block drains to. Stale (2018/2020), but the topology has not moved.

layers.label: 1-year 24-hour rainfall isopleths
layers.notes: Genuinely useful for cloudburst work and surfaced nowhere else. Carried by DEC's stormwater mapper.

layers.label: Water & sewer permits
layers.notes: No geometry of its own — join to MapPLUTO on BBL. A record of who was allowed to connect what, and when.

layers.label: Hurricane evacuation zones
layers.notes: Six zones, version 26b, revised quarterly. An administrative geography: it tells you who is told to leave, not where water goes. Pair it with the SLOSH inundation layer underneath.

layers.label: Hurricane inundation (SLOSH)
layers.notes: The National Hurricane Center's 2020 SLOSH model — NE1 basin, 10 m, surge at high tide. The physical layer under the administrative one.

layers.label: Waterfront public access areas
layers.fields: 38 columns including Chair Certification and CPC Approval dates
layers.notes: Privately owned, publicly accessible. The paperwork trail of a right of way.

layers.label: WPAA access points
layers.notes: The doors. Where a person may actually step from the street onto the water's edge.

layers.label: Human-powered boat launches
layers.notes: Sixty-three places a person may put a kayak in the water. One of the two best ethnographic hooks in the survey.

layers.label: Saltwater fishing sites
layers.notes: Who fishes where, and on whose land, is a question a map can pose and only fieldwork can answer.

layers.label: Waterfront parks
layers.notes: Filtered to WATERFRONT = true from Parks Properties. This is how you get Brooklyn Bridge Park, the East River Esplanade and Freshkills — there are no separate layers for them.

layers.label: Planimetric shoreline
layers.notes: Use this one for drawing. For analysis use the tidally coordinated shoreline instead.

layers.label: Tidally coordinated shoreline
layers.notes: Coordinated against Kings Point, Bergen West, Sandy Hook and The Battery. Use this one for analysis.

layers.label: Waterfront Revitalization Program boundary
layers.notes: Use the live service, not the 2015 shapefile cbn4-bn4p.

layers.label: Waterfront access plans
layers.notes: Where the City wrote a bespoke access rule for a stretch of shore instead of applying the general one.

layers.label: Landward coastal area boundary
layers.notes: The line that legally defines the coastal zone.

layers.label: Restrictive declaration sites
layers.notes: Waterfront public-access obligations are often recorded as deed restrictions, so this is the legal instrument sitting behind the WPAA geography.

layers.label: Special purpose districts (incl. Special Coastal Risk)
layers.notes: The Special Coastal Risk District — Zoning Resolution Article XIII Chapter 7 — should live in the nysp special-purpose feature class of this geodatabase. That is an assumption; check it on download.

layers.label: USACE navigation channels
layers.notes: Ambrose, Anchorage, Kill Van Kull, Arthur Kill. The harbour as a maintained industrial surface — and a bi-state one.

layers.label: USACE eHydro survey footprints
layers.notes: 779 dated channel-survey footprints — a record of when somebody last measured the bottom.

layers.label: Shoreline construction (NOAA chart)
layers.notes: Piers, wharves, bulkheads, seawalls. The City publishes no dataset of the structures holding its own shoreline in place — for some 520 miles of edge, everything usable comes from the navy's chartmakers. Rebuilt every Saturday night.

layers.label: Pilings (NOAA chart)
layers.notes: 1,667 pilings — the ghosts of piers otherwise gone from every map the city keeps.

layers.label: NOS hydrographic survey archive
layers.notes: 11,000+ smooth sheets from the mid-1800s onward. An archive as much as a dataset: a century and a half of successive soundings of the same harbour, which is the closest thing here to a historical bathymetry.

layers.label: The Battery tide gauge (8518750)
layers.fields: Water level, hourly height, high/low, monthly mean
layers.notes: A time series, not a map — lat 40.700554, lon −74.01417. No key required, but rate-limited: budget for throttling. The record behind every sea-level number on this site.

layers.label: Building elevation & subgrade
layers.fields: z_grade, z_floor (first-floor elevation, NAVD88 ft), subgrade basement flag
layers.notes: 861,876 building points. The only layer that lets a student compute freeboard — first-floor elevation minus base flood elevation. Rendered as a probe layer: a real fill over this many features crashes the renderer, so MapLibre downloads the tiles, draws none, and it stays queryable.

layers.label: Resiliency exposure forecast — coastal flooding
layers.notes: NTA-level and without geometry of its own — join NTA_Code to the 2020 Neighborhood Tabulation Areas service. Compares a Control Scenario, with no coastal protection, against a Planned Action Scenario. The City costing its own future.

layers.label: Flood vulnerability index
layers.fields: fshri (12 socioeconomic indicators), ss_cur / ss_50s / ss_80s storm surge, tid_20s / tid_50s / tid_80s tidal
layers.notes: By census tract. Every field ships as text — cast before you compare.

layers.label: Historically redlined areas (HOLC)
layers.notes: Put this under the floodplain and over the environmental justice areas. Three layers, one publisher, one argument.

layers.label: Federal disadvantaged communities (CEJST)
layers.notes: The federal definition, beside the city's and the state's. Where the three disagree is where the politics is.

layers.label: NYCHA developments
layers.notes: Public housing against the floodplain is the single most-cited overlay in the Sandy literature, and it is one layer away here.

layers.label: Heat vulnerability index
layers.notes: The other climate hazard. Heat and flood vulnerability do not fall on the same blocks, and the difference is worth an afternoon.

layers.label: Peaker plants
layers.notes: Fired up on the hottest days, sited where objection was cheapest. Peakers, bus depots and last-mile warehouses together are the standard EJ triad.

layers.label: Last-mile warehouses
layers.notes: The newest layer of the industrial waterfront, and the one arriving fastest.

layers.label: NY Rising community reconstruction areas
layers.notes: In New York City these were digitised from neighbourhoods and business recovery zones, then adjusted by Community Planning Committees using damage assessments. An administratively drawn neighbourhood boundary, produced by committee in response to a flood, still marked preliminary.

layers.label: NFIP redacted claims
layers.notes: Tabular and redacted to census tract, filterable server-side by countyCode. Where insurance actually paid, as against where the maps say it should have. A working reference implementation exists at github.com/mebauer/nfip-datasets.

layers.label: NFIP policies in force
layers.notes: Who is insured, beside who claimed. The ratio is a map of confidence.

layers.label: NYC wetlands
layers.notes: Explicitly carries no jurisdictional authority. For regulatory wetlands go to NYSDEC — and then read what DEC says about its own maps.

layers.label: Land cover, 6-inch (2017)
layers.notes: 1.33 GB and eight classes. Downsample to 1–5 m or aggregate to polygons before you go anywhere near a browser.

layers.label: Impervious surface (2020)
layers.notes: 4.96 GB. Do not load raw — join the percentage to MapPLUTO on BBL instead.

layers.label: DEC regulatory tidal wetlands
layers.notes: Layer 1, not 0. Troy Dam to the tip of Staten Island.

layers.label: DEC coastal erosion hazard areas
layers.notes: DEC says explicitly this is an initial screening tool only, and that the legal boundaries are the paper maps filed with municipalities. A good teaching point about the gap between a shapefile and a regulation.

layers.label: DEC informational freshwater wetlands
layers.notes: Layer 2. 310,908 polygons statewide — clip before you do anything. Non-regulatory.

layers.label: DEC previously mapped freshwater wetlands
layers.notes: Where the 2022 Act moved the jurisdiction line. The difference between this and the current layer is the reform, drawn.

layers.label: DEC remediation parcels (brownfields)
layers.notes: Updated nightly. Intersect with the floodplain for the toxic-sites-in-the-flood-zone exercise. Small; tiles beautifully.

layers.label: Harbor water quality
layers.notes: 98,288 measurements, 43 columns, and no coordinates. The schema carries a sampling-location code and no geometry: a century-old sampling programme whose measurements are public and whose places are not. Listed here so the absence is visible rather than silently omitted.

layers.label: Beach water samples (enterococci)
layers.notes: Joins on beach name. The one water-quality series with a place attached, and the one that closes beaches.

layers.label: DOHMH waterways indicators (NTA)
layers.fields: Dissolved oxygen, bacteria, aggregated to neighbourhood tabulation area
layers.notes: The practical route to mapping harbour water quality without first solving the station-geometry problem.

layers.label: Hyperlocal temperature sensors
layers.notes: Roughly 475 street sensors reporting hourly — the same distributed-sensor model as FloodNet, pointed at heat instead of water.

layers.label: Topobathymetric DEM, 1 m (2017)
layers.notes: Green and near-infrared lidar with bathymetry integrated, so it does not stop at the waterline — the only elevation product here that describes the bottom as well as the bank. exportTilesAllowed is false: rendering service only. For files, use the NOAA product.

layers.label: Topobathy lidar DEM, 1 ft (2017) — tiles
layers.notes: 31 GeoTIFF tiles, EPSG:6539 horizontal and 6360 vertical, collected May–July 2017. Clip via the Digital Coast Data Access Viewer rather than pulling the bulk S3 prefix. No access constraints.

layers.label: USGS 3DEP elevation
layers.notes: Free of charge and without use restrictions — the cleanest licence in the whole survey, and the only elevation source that covers both states uniformly.

layers.label: NYC orthoimagery
layers.scenarioNote: Ten epochs from 2006 to 2024, per borough. Step through them over a stretch of shore and the landfill, the buyout, and the new bulkhead all become visible without a single attribute. Registration is no longer required — the Clearinghouse dropped password protection in January 2023.

layers.label: NYC Ferry landings
layers.notes: From stops.txt in the GTFS feed. The only explicit licence found anywhere in this survey, and it is the most restrictive of the lot — revocable, non-transferable, non-assignable. The federal navy-chart data is freer than the city's ferry timetable.

layers.label: NYC Ferry routes
layers.notes: From shapes.txt. The waterborne commute, which is also the evacuation route nobody plans around.

layers.label: Piers, wharves, bulkheads, seawalls, revetments, riprap
layers.notes: Catalogue queries for 'pier marine terminal bulkhead', 'landing terminal dock' and 'marina boat launch kayak dock' all return zero. For a city with some 520 miles of shoreline, the structures holding the edge in place are absent from the municipal commons. Everything usable comes from the NOAA chart layers in this site.

source.why: no City dataset exists; use the NOAA ENC layers instead

layers.label: 2021 Comprehensive Waterfront Plan GIS
layers.notes: A 155 MB PDF and six topic PDFs. The City's principal waterfront planning document is not machine-readable.

layers.label: Coastal protection project alignments
layers.notes: No official geometry for any of them. East Side Coastal Resiliency: the only vector data sits on a personal ArcGIS account from 2022 — usable as a teaching artefact, not a source of record. Lower Manhattan Coastal Resiliency: one JPEG. Living Breakwaters: a completed $111M structure in the harbour with no published alignment.

layers.label: Staten Island Sandy buyout footprints
layers.notes: Oakwood Beach, Ocean Breeze and Graham Beach are not published as state GIS. Probably the most ethnographically loaded flood geography in the city, and it has no shapefile.

layers.label: CSO outfalls, sewer mains, regulators, interceptors
layers.notes: Catch basins and MS4 outfalls are the only sewer geometry the City releases. The volunteer Open Sewer Atlas reconstructs 4,850 CSO and stormwater outfalls, distributed by email request and labelled NOT OFFICIAL — infrastructure the utility maps but does not publish.

source.why: unpublished; partial volunteer reconstruction at openseweratlas.tumblr.com

layers.label: Bluebelt and Cloudburst programme boundaries
layers.notes: Both programmes exist only as prose and PDFs.

layers.label: MTA and Port Authority flood and resilience geodata
layers.notes: The two agencies with the most flood-exposed infrastructure in the harbour publish PDFs.

layers.label: Significant Maritime and Industrial Areas
layers.notes: Seven polygons defining the working waterfront, distributed by Local Area Network access. You email wrp@planning.nyc.gov.

layers.label: 1609 shoreline and landfill extent
layers.notes: No published vector for either. The Welikia Map Explorer shows the 1609 landscape — 33,209 clickable blocks built from 614 georeferenced historical maps — but it is viewable, not downloadable. NYPL holds 7,799 digitised historical maps and a Map Warper toolkit: students can trace a shoreline, and nobody has published the traces. Warning: NYC Open Data's Landfills dataset 6gvx-hydd is solid-waste landfills — a naming collision worth flagging.

source.why: no published vector; traceable from NYPL scans

layers.label: USACE NY & NJ Harbor and Tributaries Study (HATS)
layers.notes: Reached Draft Final / State and Agency Review in March 2026 and is not public. Scope has narrowed from a basin-wide barrier study to near-term Actionable Elements at Oakwood Beach, Harlem River and East Riser. PDFs and a StoryMap only; no GIS.

parked_note: Nothing parked. Parking a layer is moving one entry from `layers` into `parked` — the app reads only `layers`.
